content:
Three o'clock in the morning. Adelaide is silent, the house is dark, and the only thing that exists is the pain, which has settled behind my right eye with the focused intensity of a blowtorch applied to the inside of my skull.

Cluster headaches. The literature calls them among the most painful conditions known to humanity. The nickname is suicide headaches, and it's descriptive rather than metaphorical. People kill themselves during these attacks, and not because they've lost the will to live in any philosophical sense. The pain becomes extreme enough that the body's arithmetic flips and death becomes preferable to continuation. That's a physical computation.

I'm in month six of the longest lockdown in Australian history - Melbourne is, strictly; Adelaide's restrictions are lighter and the isolation is real all the same - and the solitude has given me time with questions I usually keep in motion. When you're busy you can outrun them. When the world stops and the pain arrives and it's three in the morning, there's nothing between you and the question.

The question is whether, if there's a designer, my nervous system stands as the counter-argument.

I want to engage honestly, which means saying where I start. I grew up in Adelaide and attended Prince Alfred College, a school with a Uniting Church affiliation and chapel services I attended regularly without believing much of what was said in them. My household wasn't religious. God wasn't a presence at home. He was a presence at school, in the architecture and the hymns and the solemn language of assembly, and I found the architecture beautiful and the hymns moving and the language interesting without ever quite believing there was someone on the other end of the line.

Atheism strikes me as a claim of certainty the evidence doesn't support. Whether there's a God, a designer, a consciousness behind the machinery - nobody knows. The honest position, respecting both the limits of human knowledge and the genuine strangeness of existence, is uncertainty. I'm agnostic and I hold it seriously, as an intellectual commitment rather than a polite hedge. I don't have enough information to be certain, and pretending otherwise in either direction seems to me a failure of honesty.

What I can say with the authority of direct experience is that pain of this magnitude poses a problem for any theology beginning with a benevolent designer.

**Taking the Arguments Seriously**

The people who hold these arguments aren't stupid and many are considerably smarter than I am. The theological tradition that wrestles with suffering is thousands of years old and has produced responses of genuine depth. They deserve engagement.

Free will. The argument that a universe capable of genuine moral agency must also be capable of suffering, because freedom requires the possibility of harm. This is coherent and I understand it. Cluster headaches result from nobody's free will. They're a neurological malfunction, a misfiring of the trigeminal nerve, a biological error with no moral dimension at all. Nobody chose this and nobody's freedom is enhanced by it. The free will defence addresses moral suffering, the kind caused by human choices, and has nothing whatever to say about natural suffering, which is the kind I know best.

Growth through adversity. The argument that suffering builds character and deepens empathy and forges strength. I find this the most tempting and the most dangerous - tempting because there's truth in it, since I've learned things through pain I couldn't have learned otherwise, and dangerous because it comes perilously close to justifying the suffering, suggesting it was necessary or even good because of what it produced.

I reject it, and my objection is about proportionality rather than logic. You don't need a blowtorch to teach someone the value of warmth. You don't need the most painful condition in the medical literature to develop empathy. If there's a teacher behind this curriculum, the teacher is either incompetent or sadistic, and in neither case deserves the gratitude the argument implies.

The mystery. The argument that God's purposes lie beyond human comprehension, that suffering serves a function we can't see from our limited vantage, that the design is too large to be judged by creatures as small as us. This is the most honest of the theological responses because it acknowledges the problem without pretending to solve it, and it's also the emptiest, because it can justify anything at all. Any amount of suffering, any degree of cruelty, any injustice can be waved away with the claim that the purposes are mysterious. The argument amounts to a surrender dressed as humility.

I've sat with all of these at three in the morning, when the pain is at its worst and the philosophical distance between suffering and theodicy has collapsed to zero. In those moments the arguments stop being interesting and become insulting. Their internal logic holds up fine. They simply ask me to value the explanation above the experience. To trust the brochure when the product is demonstrably broken.

I've spent enough time navigating broken systems, healthcare and institutional and the slow machinery of Australian bureaucracy, to know what that particular form of trust costs. It costs your ability to see clearly. It costs your capacity for honest assessment. It costs, in the end, your grip on reality, because reality is the thing in front of you rather than the explanation offered for it.

**The Same Apparatus**

I want to complicate the picture now, because the picture deserves it.

The same nervous system that produces the agony produces everything else. The sunset in Kyoto that stopped me mid-step and held me there while the light turned the temple gardens into something that felt more real than real. The music that sometimes, for reasons I can't explain, makes the world briefly cohere into something resembling meaning. The taste of food prepared by someone who cared about preparing it. The click of comprehension, the moment a pattern that was invisible becomes visible and the world rearranges around the new seeing.

All of it comes from the same apparatus. The same neurons, the same chemistry. The system that tortures me also gives me everything worth having.

None of that points to design. If anything it points to indifference. The system wasn't built for me and it wasn't built for anything. It processes, it responds, it generates experience as a byproduct of complexity, and the experience includes both agony and beauty because the system doesn't distinguish between them. It produces both with equal facility and no apparent preference.

I find that strangely liberating. If the system is indifferent then the suffering carries no message, no test, no lesson, no hand of God pressing me into shape. Just pain. And pain stripped of meaning is easier to bear than pain that's supposed to mean something, because meaningful pain carries the extra burden of interpretation. Why me. What's the lesson. What am I meant to learn. Those questions are natural and understandable and they add a layer of suffering on top of the suffering. Remove the meaning and the layer goes with it.

I can't claim there's a God and I can't claim there isn't. What I can claim is that I don't know, that the not-knowing is the honest position, and that from inside the not-knowing it remains entirely possible to build a life that means something even where the meaning is constructed rather than received.

The values I hold - honesty, compassion, treating people with dignity, pursuing understanding for its own sake - belong to no religion exclusively and appear in most of them. Christianity offers them. Hinduism offers them. The secular humanist tradition offers them. I take them where I find them and I don't worry much about the metaphysical packaging they arrive in. A good value is a good value whether it was delivered by a prophet or a philosopher or a parent or by the hard experience of suffering that teaches you, against your will, what it means to need kindness and not receive it.

At three in the morning, with the pain at its peak and the world reduced to the space between my skull and the pillow, theology offers no comfort. What comforts, to the extent that anything does, is simpler: the knowledge that this attack will end. Not permanently. This one will end, and when it does the world will still be there, and in the world there will be things worth experiencing, and the experiencing is the whole point. The sunset. The music. The taste of food. The click of understanding.

Meaning is built by hand, in pain, without guarantee. And the building is the thing.
